title: Long‐term reduction of invasive killer shrimp (Dikerogammarus villosus) density following removal of zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha) shells and coarse substrate on UK lake beds
content:
Working with Citizen Scientists, researchers tested manual removal of coarse cobbles and zebra mussel shells from fine-sediment lake beds to reduce invasive killer shrimp densities. Killer shrimp use these features for habitat, and after clearing them from 3 × 3 m sections of lakebed, killer shrimp densities were reduced by over 90% in these sections, and remained low across the multi-year study. This method is cheap, fast and potentially scalable across similar environments invaded by killer shrimp, provided careful evaluation of risk from non-target impacts on native freshwater ecology.


Abstract

Control strategies for invasive non-native species can be infeasibly costly for environmental managers and are frequently unsuccessful. Rapid, low-cost and lasting management strategies are urgently required. The Ponto-Caspian amphipod Dikerogammarus villosus, or ‘killer shrimp’, is a prolific invasive species across Europe, of special governmental concern for UK biodiversity. Current D. villosus management techniques have shown mixed success and are not financially or practically scalable. We evaluated the efficacy of low-cost, manual clearance of coarse substrate and zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha) shells to reduce D. villosus densities in invaded lakes. We conducted experiments, supported by Citizen Scientists, where localised patches of coarse substrate and zebra mussel shells, known to be favoured habitat for D. villosus, were cleared from two sites in the Norfolk and Suffolk Broads, UK. Responses of D. villosus and native macroinvertebrate communities were monitored at these sites over 2 years. Clearances significantly reduced local D. villosus abundance by >90% and >96% (coarse substrate and shell patches, respectively). Changes were observed within 3 months of intervention, with D. villosus densities remaining suppressed on cleared patches throughout 2-year monitoring periods. Cobble clearances had no significant impact on native invertebrate communities, indicating this method selectively targeted invasive D. villosus. However, D. polymorpha clearance also reduced native macroinvertebrate abundance and richness, likely due to general facilitative effects of the bivalves. Our findings identify that coarse substrate and D. polymorpha shell clearances, suitable for Citizen Science activities, can provide a rapid, effective method to manage invasive D. villosus. Solution: Coarse substrate and D. polymorpha shell clearance could be deployed at low cost to reduce D. villosus densities in hotspot areas of invasive species vectoring, such as marinas, fishing platforms and reservoirs. Application could reduce both local impacts of D. villosus and the probability of wider spread. Substrate modification impact on native communities appeared context-dependent; therefore, trade-offs when using this approach for INNS management will need to be considered at a site-specific scale. Engagement with Citizen Scientist groups may facilitate rapid use of substrate modification at other sites in response to D. villosus introductions, with theoretical scalability for wider application.
